newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German asset revaluation debate enters final round.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German asset revaluation debate enters final round.

text.p: The Bundesbank said on Thursday it expected to soon hammer out the final details of a compromise plan on revaluing German official reserves, ending a painful chapter in its relations with Bonn.

Meeting for the first time since rejecting a government scheme to revalue German gold and currency assets, the Bundesbank sounded a reserved, but unmistakably triumphant note, saying any deal would reflect its original objections.

"Based on the results of talks so far the central bank council sees good prospects for a solution which takes account of the fundamental position it outlined in its statement on May 28," the Bundesbank said.

Two weeks ago Germany's two leading economic policy-makers openly quarrelled over Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plans to revalue Bundesbank gold and currency reserves at higher, market influenced levels.
The Bundesbank sharply criticised the scheme as an attack on its independence and a move which would threaten market confidence in the future European single currency, the euro.

The debate seriously shook financial market confidence in Germany's preparations for European economic and monetary union (EMU) and offered a rare view of the cental bank's power in guiding economic policy.

Under pressure from the highly-respected Bundesbank and opposition politicians, Waigel was forced to seek a face-saving compromise -- the broad outlines of which have already been reached in talks with Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer.

Under the deal, the Bundesbank would revalue part of its currency reserves in 1997 and make a special payout in 1998 to the Inherited Debt Redemption Fund, thereby helping to reduce Germany's public debt.
Such a payout, however, would come too late to help Germany reduce its debt in 1997 -- the key year for deciding which nations can join EMU, scheduled to start in January 1999.
The revaluation is not expected to affect the Bundesbank's gold reserves.
Analysts played down any worries the talks may cause financial markets.
"The revaluation issue has been pushed into the background," said Timo Klein, economist at MMS International. "The market's main focus is already on the Amsterdam summit (June 16 and 17)."
He and others said the upcoming talks between the Bundesbank and finance ministry will now turn on at what level currency reserves could be revalued and when the profits could be transfered.
Balance sheet law allows foreign exchange reserves to be valued at a level higher than the all-time low, but no higher than the purchase price.

With the central bank's dollars valued at the lowest ever Frankfurt fixing rate for the dollar of 1.3620 marks, the government at least in theory could post a major profit by valuing those holdings at higher levels.

Allan Saunderson, chief economic analyst at S.G. Money Research in Frankfurt said that if the average purchase price were between 1.55 to 1.60 marks, currencies could provide more than 10 billion marks in hidden reserves.
At least some on the Bundesbank council, however, may still feel that revaluation amounts to an accounting trick and could put up a fight before agreeing to a final deal with Bonn.
Analysts said, however, that Bundesbank council members should quickly fall into line and that a final deal should be reached within a couple of weeks.
"Tietmeyer will not want to see the Bundesbank overplay its hand,' Saunderson said. "He will get his way and we will soon see a final resolution."
